title: Cost of Studying in Ireland for Indian Students: Trinity, UCD and Financial Proof Rules

runs.t: The cost of studying in Ireland depends on the university, course, level of study, accommodation and lifestyle. Indian students should budget for tuition, living costs, private medical insurance, visa and registration costs where applicable, travel and initial accommodation deposits. The financial evidence required for immigration is a separate minimum test and should not be mistaken for a complete personal budget.

Use the exact tuition fee published for the programme and intake, add a realistic accommodation and living budget, and demonstrate the required funds through acceptable documentary evidence. For courses longer than eight months, the current student finance guidance requires evidence of immediate access to at least €10,000 for one academic year, in addition to tuition and funding for subsequent years.

Trinity College Dublin and University College Dublin (UCD) publish course-specific fees. Fees can differ significantly by school, programme, student category and academic year. Do not use a university-wide average as the price of a particular master’s programme.

sections.title: Financial proof for an Irish study visa

runs.t: For academic courses beginning after 1 July 2023, the current ISD guidance requires visa-required students to show evidence of immediate access to at least €10,000 for one academic year. For each subsequent year of a multi-year course, the student and/or sponsor must demonstrate ready access to at least €10,000 in addition to the course fees for that year.

For courses with a duration of less than eight months, the required amount is €833 per month of stay or €6,665, whichever is lower. The applicant must show that they can support themselves without relying on public funds or casual employment.
An up-to-date bank statement showing transactions over the previous six months.
The account holder’s name, address, account number and account type.
An explanation and supporting evidence for large or irregular deposits, such as education loans, sale proceeds or savings certificate encashment.
If using a deposit or savings account, a bank letter confirming that the funds can be accessed.
Where a sponsor is paying, evidence of the relationship, sponsor’s income and ability to support the student, plus the sponsor’s bank statements.
Proof of tuition payment or the funds available to pay tuition, according to the application requirements.
Private medical insurance evidence; the institution may arrange cover, but the acceptance letter should confirm this if so.

Credit cards are not accepted as proof of finances under the published guidance. Applicants should follow the current visa application checklist and ensure that every document is genuine, complete and consistent.

sections.title: Education bond alternative for eligible degree students

runs.t: ISD describes a pilot alternative finance method for degree-programme students: an education bond with a minimum value of €10,000 lodged with an approved student fees payment service. The bond must remain in place from the initial visa application until immigration registration. The receipt may be accepted as evidence, but the visa officer can still request additional financial documents. ISD is not a party to the student’s contract with the bond provider.

sections.title: Dublin, Cork and Galway living-cost comparison

runs.t: Use a current and consistent data source. RTB/ESRI rent index data is based on registered tenancy data and distinguishes new and existing tenancies; it is not a direct measure of student residence fees or room listings. In the RTB’s Q4 2025 update, average rents for existing tenancies were highest in Dublin City (€1,875), followed by Cork City (€1,413) and Galway City (€1,409). These figures describe standardised average rents for existing tenancies, not the price of a student room.
Avoid converting the RTB city figures into an assumed per-student cost.

sections.title: Example budget structure for an Indian student

runs.t: A useful planning model should calculate the first-year cash requirement separately from the total programme cost. First-year cash requirement = tuition due before enrolment + required financial proof + visa/registration/insurance costs + travel + accommodation deposit and initial rent. The student should then model later-year tuition and living costs, including the source of funds for each year.

faq.q: Is €10,000 enough to study in Ireland?

runs.t: €10,000 is the current minimum immediate-access living-funds requirement for a visa-required student on a course longer than eight months. It is separate from tuition and may be below the student’s actual living costs.

faq.q: Do I need to show €10,000 every year?

runs.t: For each subsequent year of a multi-year course, the guidance requires evidence of ready access to at least €10,000 in addition to that year’s course fees.

faq.q: Can an education loan be used as proof of funds?

runs.t: A loan may be relevant evidence, but the applicant must provide documentary proof of the funds and explain large or irregular deposits. Follow the current ISD evidence requirements.

faq.q: Are Trinity and UCD fees the same for all master’s courses?

runs.t: No. Fees are programme-specific and can change by academic year and student category. Check the exact course fee page.

faq.q: Can I work part-time to meet the financial requirement?

runs.t: No. Students must demonstrate they can support themselves without relying on casual employment. Stamp 2 work permission is subject to separate weekly-hour limits.
